concepts.name: Treaty of Surat (1775): Validity and Contested Authority
key_dimensions: Circumstances of signing — Raghunathrao's contested claim to Peshwaship and British opportunism
Bombay Council's unilateral action vs. Calcutta Council's authority under the Regulating Act 1773
Why Calcutta Council repudiated the treaty — administrative and political implications
Connection to the First Anglo-Maratha War as a trigger event

concepts.name: Convention of Wadgaon (1779): Humiliation and Repudiation
key_dimensions: Circumstances — British military defeat and forced concession to the Marathas
Terms: British agreement to restore all territories acquired since 1773
Repudiation by Governor-General Warren Hastings and its diplomatic consequences
Significance as the only major British military humiliation in the Anglo-Maratha Wars

concepts.name: Treaty of Salbai (1782): Consolidation and Strategic Pause
key_dimensions: Key terms: Status quo ante, British recognition of Madhavrao II as Peshwa, Raghunathrao pensioned off
Significance: Secured British position against Hyder Ali by neutralizing Maratha threat
22-year peace period and its role in British consolidation in the Deccan
Comparison with Treaty of Surat — shift from opportunism to strategic stability

concepts.name: Battle of Kharda (1795): Last Maratha Victory and Internal Decline
key_dimensions: Marathas vs. Nizam — significance as the last major Maratha confederacy military success
Internal contradiction: Victory followed by rapid political disintegration within the confederacy
Role of Nana Fadnavis in orchestrating the campaign
Contrast with subsequent Maratha military performance against the British

concepts.name: Treaty of Bassein (1802): The Subsidiary Alliance and Peshwa's Surrender
key_dimensions: Circumstances: Peshwa Baji Rao II's defeat at Poona by Holkar, flight to British protection
Key terms: Subsidiary alliance, British troops stationed in Maratha territory, Peshwa's loss of sovereignty
Why it was a turning point — it divided the Maratha confederacy against itself
Comparison with other subsidiary alliances (Hyderabad 1798, Awadh 1801) — similarities and unique features
Maratha chiefs' (Scindia, Bhonsle, Holkar) reaction and trigger for Second Anglo-Maratha War

concepts.name: Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05): Military Campaigns and Key Battles
key_dimensions: Two-front strategy: Arthur Wellesley in the Deccan, Lake in the north
Battle of Assaye (1803) — Wellesley's decisive but costly victory over Scindia-Bhonsle forces
Battle of Laswari (1803) — Lake's defeat of Scindia's forces, capture of Delhi and Agra
Battle of Argaon/Argaum — Wellesley's second major engagement against Bhonsle
Strategic outcome: British control over Delhi, Agra, Orissa, and Broach

concepts.name: Treaties Ending the Second Anglo-Maratha War: Scindia, Bhonsle, and Holkar
key_dimensions: Treaty of Deogaon (1803) with Bhonsle — cession of Cuttack (Orissa) and Berar regions
Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon (1803) with Scindia — cession of territories in Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Broach, and Ahmednagar
Treaty of Rajghat (1805) with Holkar — relatively lenient terms, Holkar not fully defeated
Comparison: Why Holkar got better terms than Scindia and Bhonsle — Cornwallis's recall and policy reversal

concepts.name: Role of Governor-Generals in Anglo-Maratha Wars: Policy Shifts
key_dimensions: Warren Hastings: Aggressive Bombay Council, repudiation of Wadgaon, Treaty of Salbai — defensive consolidation
Wellesley (Richard): Offensive use of Subsidiary Alliance at Bassein, engineering Second Anglo-Maratha War
Cornwallis (second term) and Barlow: Reversal of Wellesley's aggressive policy — Treaty of Rajghat's leniency
Hastings (Francis Rawdon): Final destruction of Maratha power in Third War — contrast with earlier governors

concepts.name: Maratha Confederacy's Internal Divisions: Structural Weakness
key_dimensions: Five chiefs: Peshwa, Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Bhonsle (Nagpur), Gaekwad (Baroda) — rivalries
Peshwa's declining authority vs. rising power of Scindia and Holkar
Why the confederacy never united against the British — Gaekwad's early alliance with British, Peshwa's betrayal
Comparison with Sikh confederacy — similar internal fragmentation exploited by British

concepts.name: Nana Fadnavis: Diplomat, Strategist, and the Last Maratha Bulwark
key_dimensions: Role as de facto regent during Peshwa Madhavrao II's minority and Sawai Madhavrao's reign
Diplomatic skills: Preventing French-Maratha alliance while managing British pressure
Nana Fadnavis's death (1800) as a turning point — 'the last of the Marathas' (British assessment)
Contrast with Baji Rao II's incompetence — why leadership vacuum accelerated Maratha decline

concepts.name: Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–18): Triggers and the Pindari Connection
key_dimensions: Pindari menace as the stated British pretext — who were the Pindaris and their link to Maratha chiefs
Hastings's (Francis Rawdon) grand strategy: Simultaneous encirclement of Pindaris and Marathas
Why the war was virtually inevitable — British encirclement policy and Maratha loss of strategic space
Triple threat: Pindari suppression + Maratha war + Hyderabad subsidiary alliance consolidation

concepts.name: Key Battles of the Third Anglo-Maratha War: Kirkee, Sitabaldi, and Mahidpur
key_dimensions: Battle of Kirkee (1817) — defeat of Peshwa Baji Rao II near Poona, flight of the Peshwa
Battle of Sitabaldi (1817) — Bhonsle of Nagpur's forces defeated; significance for central India
Battle of Mahidpur (1817) — decisive defeat of Holkar of Indore by Malcolm
UPSC trap: Matching correct battles with correct Maratha chiefs and outcomes

concepts.name: Treaties Ending the Third Anglo-Maratha War: Final Dismemberment
key_dimensions: Treaty of Poona (1817) — Peshwa accepts humiliating terms before the war; prewar concessions
Treaty of Mandasor (1818) — Holkar's submission, Rajput states placed under British protection
Treaty of Nagpur (1816/1818) — Bhonsle's territories and Central Provinces arrangement
Abolition of the Peshwaship (1818) — Baji Rao II pensioned off to Bithur; end of Maratha political power

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance System: Application and Impact on Marathas
key_dimensions: Mechanics of the subsidiary alliance — British troops, annual subsidy, no independent foreign policy
Gaekwad of Baroda (1802) as the first Maratha chief to accept; strategic implications for confederacy unity
How Bassein (1802) differed from standard subsidiary alliances — it installed a claimant to power
Long-term impact: Financial drain on Maratha states, displacement of Maratha soldiers (Pindari problem)

concepts.name: Pindaris: Origins, Operations, and Suppression
key_dimensions: Composition: Irregular cavalry of mixed origin attached to Maratha armies — not a separate tribe
Leaders: Chitu, Wasil Muhammad, Karim Khan — operating from Malwa and Deccan
British strategy: Pincer movement under Hastings coordinating three separate armies (1817–18)
Outcome: Chitu killed by tiger, Wasil Muhammad and Karim Khan surrendered — fate of each leader

concepts.name: Arthur Wellesley's Military Campaigns in the Deccan: Tactics and Legacy
key_dimensions: Wellesley's logistical innovations — supply chain management as key to success at Assaye
Battle of Assaye (1803): Wellesley's own assessment — 'the bloodiest for the numbers' he ever fought
Capture of Seringapatam (1799) vs. Deccan campaigns — continuity in Wellesley's India strategy
Wellesley's Deccan experience and its influence on his Peninsular War tactics in Europe

concepts.name: Raghunathrao (Raghoba) Dispute: Dynastic Crisis as British Entry Point
key_dimensions: Raghunathrao's assassination of Peshwa Narayanrao (1773) and disputed succession
Raghoba's appeal to British Bombay Council — why British found it strategically useful
Nana Fadnavis and the Maratha regency council opposing Raghoba — legitimate vs. British-backed claimant
Parallel with other British interventions in succession disputes (Mysore, Awadh) — pattern recognition

concepts.name: Maratha Military Reforms and European Officers: Strengths and Limitations
key_dimensions: Scindia's European-trained infantry under De Boigne and Perron — formidable but dependent
Why European officers abandoned or defected during the Second Anglo-Maratha War
Holkar's irregular cavalry tactics vs. Scindia's European-style infantry — contrasting military philosophies
Fundamental weakness: European-style army without European administrative and financial infrastructure

concepts.name: Consequences of the Anglo-Maratha Wars: Territorial and Political Outcomes
key_dimensions: British territorial gains: Orissa, Doab, Rajputana suzerainty, Central India, Deccan
End of Mughal pensioner status — British became de facto sovereigns of Delhi after 1803
Creation of Central India Agency and Rajputana Agency — administrative reorganization of acquired territories
Long-term: Maratha soldiers' displacement → Pindari problem → pretext for further British expansion

concepts.name: Comparison of Three Anglo-Maratha Wars: Causes, Outcomes, and British Strategy Evolution
key_dimensions: First War (1775–82): Defensive/opportunistic — ends in stalemate (Salbai); British learning phase
Second War (1803–05): Offensive subsidiary alliance strategy — major territorial gains; Wellesley's aggression
Third War (1817–18): Final annihilation strategy — complete end of Maratha political independence
UPSC trap: Governors-General, key treaties, and territorial outcomes mixed across all three wars
